header.title: Sermones Ad Populum. Sermonum Quorundam Ex Fragmentis: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Augustine, Saint
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0040.stoa013h.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa013h.opp-l: Line 1: the final clause reads 'si volo, et possum, nec Dei adjutorio possum'; as printed it is odd, and 'nec' may be corrupt (one would expect 'et sine Dei adjutorio possum', 'I can do it even without God's help'). Translated literally. Line 2: section number 'I.' read as '2.'. Line 4: 'ne remaneas Xeniis, quia impediris' is evidently corrupt; the intended word after 'remaneas' cannot be recovered with confidence (perhaps 'inanis' or 'vacuus', 'empty-handed'), shown as [...]. Line 5: 'absoluta est, scd confessio, quasi correctio ipsa est absoluta' is awkward and possibly corrupt; the sense seems to be that Pelagius' confession, taken as a correction, was what the bishops (at Diospolis, 415) acquitted. Psalm numbers follow the Vulgate as given.

Several evident scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'apemur' read as 'aperitur', 'Colera' as 'Caetera', 'tgenum' as 'egenum', 'dal' as 'dat'). The citation 'I Cor. III, 7, 8' should be 1 Cor. 12:7-8, and 'Psal. CILII' Ps. 142 (Vulgate). In section 2 'Non attendat' may be for 'attendas' ('do not heed'). In section 3 the sentence 'sic est homo ante se sub divo... quomodo itus in cubiculo' is garbled; read as 'a man is in the open air as he is in a bedroom', i.e. sees nothing; '(a)' is an editorial footnote mark. The final sentences of the last line ('Creeping things of living souls. The power of the sacrament is charity.') appear to be headings for the next section.

In the first passage, 'pisces manducare' lacks a verb of possibility for the contrast; '[yet everyone can]' supplies the evident sense (the edition's footnote mark (a) stands here). 'celos magnos' read as 'cetos magnos' (whales). 'prophetiae fides' taken as 'prophecy, faith'. 'pudoris arce' (citadel of shame) is literal; the sense is the forehead, seat of modesty.

Sermon on Faustus: 'Minare' read as 'Nomina' (name); 'Sciatis eum deseri amalis, suscipiatura vobis' read as 'Sentiat eum deseri a malis, suscipi a vobis' (uncertain); 'diC- ferre' as 'differre'; 'Hora Dona' as 'hora nona'. 'Majoratum' is uncertain: perhaps a civic office or rank Faustus renounced. The citation 'Rom. xiv, 4' should be Rom. 14:1. Quadratus is presumably the African martyr whose feast Augustine preached on.

Line 25: 'sa occidit in corde' is likely a scan error for 'se occidit' ('he kills himself in the heart', i.e. the persecutor harms his own soul); some read 'te occidit' ('he kills you in the heart'). Line 23: 'Ergo non est malum correptio si sit' is obscure and may be corrupt. Line 28: 'clausa dissolvit' is literally 'unloosed what was shut'. Line 29: 'quo genus' read as 'quod genus'; 'Qui factus est ei' as printed (Vulgate 'factus est ei').
At 30 the scanned 'per ullum saeerdotem' is read as 'per unum sacerdotem', and the heading at ab25 'lUm' as 'Item'.

nodes.text: FRAGMENTS OF CERTAIN SERMONS OF ST AURELIUS AUGUSTINE WHICH ARE STILL MISSING, FOUND IN THE COLLECTIONS OF EUGIPPIUS, BEDE, FLORUS AND JOHN, DEACON OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.
From the Sermon against the Pelagians, in Eugippius, volume 2, chapter 287 or 288 (a).

1. Bishop Urbanus. The error of the Pelagians: that temptations can be overcome by the powers of free will, and that the Lord's Prayer does not deal with temptations to sin. Those two [petitions], Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors, and, Lead us not into temptation (Matt. 6:12 and 13): when they are put to the Pelagians, what do you think they answer? I shuddered, my brothers, when I heard it. I did not hear it with my own ears, but our holy brother and fellow bishop Urbanus, who was a presbyter here and is now bishop of Sicca, when he had returned from the city of Rome, [reported that] there he clashed with someone who held such views, or [rather] he related that he had clashed [with him]; when [that man] was being pressed by the weight of the Lord's Prayer (for [Urbanus] was pressing him, and saying, 'If it is in our power not to sin, and it is in our power to overcome all temptations to sin by the powers of our will alone, why do we say to God, Lead us not into temptation?'), what do you think he answered? 'We ask God,' he said, 'not to lead us into temptation, so that we may not suffer some evil which we do not have in our power: that I may not fall from my horse and break my leg, that a robber may not kill me, and anything of that kind. For these things,' he said, 'I do not have in my power; but to overcome the temptations to my sins, if I will, I both can, and I cannot [do it] with God's help.'

2. The malignant heresy is refuted from the prayer commended by Christ and used for Peter. You see, brothers, how malignant a heresy [this is]; I see how you all shudder at it: beware that you are not caught. For I know the cunning and the evasions of impious men turned away from the truth, who, because they have already fallen into their own opinions, are unwilling to be defeated; take care, I beg you. For see, he found something to say: that we say, Lead us not into temptation, so that nothing may happen to us which we do not have in our power, in the way of bodily temptation. Was it for this, then, that the Lord said, Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation (Matt. 26:41)? Was he saying this: Watch and pray, that you may not break a leg, or have a headache, or run into loss? He was not saying this. But what was he saying? What he said to Peter: I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:32). I have prayed for you, he says, God to man, master to servant, teacher to disciple, physician to the sick: I have prayed for you. For what? That it may not fail. What? Your hand? Your foot? Your eye? Your tongue, through some paralysis, that is, a loosening of the limbs? No; but that your faith may not fail. According to these men, we have it in our power that our faith should not fail.

3. The prayers of the Church prove that the help of grace is necessary for us not to sin. Why is God asked on our behalf to grant us what these men say we ought not to ask of the everlasting Majesty, but have in our own power? Our blessings, my brothers, the blessings which we pronounce over you, they empty, they make void, they crush. You hear me, I believe, my brothers, when I say: 'Turning to the Lord, let us bless his name; may he grant us to persevere in his commandments, to walk in the right way of his instruction, to please him in every good work', and other such things. 'All this,' they say, 'is entirely placed in our power.' Then we wish such things for you in vain. Let us defend both ourselves and you, so that we may not bless without cause, nor you subscribe your Amen without cause. My brothers, your Amen is your signature, it is your consent, it is your assent. Lest perhaps some of them condemn both us and you, let us defend ourselves from the apostle Paul: let us see whether he wished for his people such things as we pray over you. Hear what he said in a certain place. I am saying a short thing. What do you say, O new heretic, whoever you are who hear me, if you are present? What do you say? That we have not sinning in our power in such a way that we can accomplish it without the help of divine grace? Is this what you say? 'This,' he says. So we have it in our power not to sin without God's help? 'Plainly,' he says, 'our free will suffices us for this.' What is it, then, that the Apostle says, writing to the Corinthians, We pray to God that you do nothing evil (2 Cor. 13:7)? You have attended, you have heard, you have received [it]; and because it is most plain, you have without doubt understood what the Apostle prayed. We pray, he says, to God that you do nothing evil. He could have said: We warn you to do nothing evil; we teach you to do nothing evil; we order you, we command you. Had he said this, he would indeed have said something true, because our will also does something: for our will does not do nothing, but alone it does not suffice. Yet he preferred to say, We pray, in order to commend grace itself: that they might understand that when they do nothing evil, it is not by their own will alone that they avoid evil, but that by God's help they fulfil what has been commanded.

4. By the command free will is shown, by prayer the necessity of the help of grace. So, brothers, when something is commanded, recognise the choice of the will; when what is commanded is prayed for, recognise the gift of grace. For you have both in the Scriptures: it is both commanded and prayed for; what is commanded, that is prayed for. See what I am saying. It is commanded that we understand. How is it commanded that we understand? Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding (Ps. 31:9). You have heard that it is commanded; ask that you may be able to fulfil what is commanded. 'How,' you say, 'do I ask?' Hear the Scripture. What has been commanded you? Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding. Because it is commanded, you have recognised the will; hear that it is prayed for, so that you may recognise grace: Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments (Ps. 118:73). It is commanded that we have wisdom: that it is commanded, I read. 'Where do you read it?' he says. Listen: You who are senseless among the people, and you fools, be wise at last (Ps. 93:8). Now what does he say? 'You see how God has commanded us to be wise. So wisdom is in our power?' I have already said: I have heard the command, I have recognised the will; hear the prayer, so that you may be able to recognise grace. Concerning wisdom, then, which is commanded us, let us hear what the apostle James says: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all abundantly (James 1:5). Continence is commanded us. Where is it commanded? The Apostle to Timothy: Keep yourself continent (1 Tim. 5:22). It is an order, it is a command; it must be heard, it must be done; but unless God helps, we fall short. We do indeed try to do it by the will, and the will strives somewhat; but let power not presume, unless weakness is helped. For certainly it is commanded: Keep yourself continent. Hear another place of Scripture: And when I knew, it says, that no one can be continent unless God gives it, and this itself was [a mark] of wisdom, to know whose gift this was, what, it says, did I do? I went to the Lord and besought him (Wisd. 8:21). What need is there to run through many [texts], my brothers? Whatever is commanded us, we must pray that it be fulfilled; but not in such a way that we let ourselves go and lie on our backs like sick men and say, 'Let God rain food upon our faces', so that we want to do nothing at all; and when the food has been rained upon our mouths, say even, 'Let God swallow for us.' We too must do something; we must be diligent, we must try; and give thanks for what we have been able [to do], and pray for what we have not been able [to do]. When you give thanks, you take care not to be condemned as ungrateful; but when you ask for what you do not yet have, you take care not to remain [...], because you are hindered.

5. An objection of the Pelagians. How Pelagius was acquitted. Think on these things, then, my brothers, whenever anyone comes to you and says to you: 'What then do we do, if we have nothing in our power unless God gives everything? Then God will not crown us, but will crown himself.' You see now that this comes from that vein: it is a vein, but it carries venom; for it has been bitten by the serpent, it is not sound. For this is what Satan does today: by the venoms of heretics he casts [people] out of the Church, just as then by the venom of the serpent he cast [them] out of paradise. Let no one say that that man was acquitted by the bishops: it was his confession that was acquitted, as if it were a correction, [and so] it was acquitted. For the things he said before the bishops seemed catholic; but what he wrote in his books the bishops who acquitted him did not know; and perhaps he has been corrected. For we ought not to despair of a man who perhaps preferred to join himself to the catholic faith, and fled for refuge to its grace and help; perhaps this has happened. Yet it was not the heresy that was acquitted, but the man denying the heresy, etc.
From the Sermon on the Lord's Passion, in the Collection of Bede and Florus, on Romans 5.

For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved in his life (Rom. 5:10). So Christ died for the ungodly. And Christ is God. How will the righteous man, found in the life of God, not reign, when the ungodly man was sought out by the death of God so that he might not perish? For we shall be saved in the life of God, because in our own life we were perishing. But when we hear both of the life of God and of the death of God, let us distinguish what comes from where. For he brought life to us, but he received death from us: and yet not for any desert of his own, but for us.
Likewise from the Sermon on the Lord's Passion, Bede and Florus on Romans 12.

Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 18:14). Therefore, since the Apostle warns us not to be high-minded but to agree with the humble (Rom. 12:16), let a man consider, if he can, into how great a precipice of pride he is carried if he does not agree with a humble God; and how ruinous it is for a man to bear impatiently what a just Lord has willed, if God bore patiently what an unjust enemy willed.
Likewise from the Sermon on the Passion, Bede and Florus on Romans 15.

Christ, then, is King of the Jews, under whose gentle yoke the Gentiles too have been placed for salvation; because to them it was granted by a greater mercy. The Apostle himself shows this more openly where he says, For I say that Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the fathers; but that the Gentiles glorify God for mercy (Rom. 15:8-9). For it was not owed to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs, unless the dogs, humbled to gathering the crumbs which they saw falling from their masters' table, were through that very humility exalted and made men, and so deserved to come to the table itself.
Likewise from the Sermon on the Passion, Bede and Florus on Galatians 6.

Let us too, then, glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world may be crucified to us, and we to the world (Gal. 6:14). So that we should not be ashamed of this cross, we have placed it on the forehead itself, that is, in the dwelling-place of shame.
Likewise from the Sermon on the Passion, Bede and Florus on Ephesians 4.

For it is not, as some think, that the old man is the body and the new man the soul: rather, the body is the outer man, the soul the inner. It is in the inner [man] that this oldness and newness take place. For when the Apostle said, Put off the old man and put on the new, he was not commanding that the body be laid aside, but that life be changed for the better. This, indeed, he taught next in order; for, wishing to explain what he had said, Therefore, he says, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbour (Eph. 4:22-25).
From the Sermon on the Lord's Resurrection, Bede and Florus on Romans 6.

For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So you too consider yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus. This is the sacrament in which those who are baptized experience the setting of the old life and begin the entrance of the new. Hence the same [Apostle] says: We were therefore buried with him through Baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6:10, 11, 4). Through this sacrament let us recognize that we have both died to sin with Christ and live to righteousness in Christ. In the cross is the pain of those who confess; in the burial, the rest of those absolved; in the resurrection, the life of the righteous.
From the Sermon for the Octave of Easter, among the Collectanea of John the Deacon on Genesis, not yet published (a).
Gen. ch. 1, v. 3. Light made.

1. And God said, Let there be light; and light was made, etc. By the name of light we understand, by allegory, all the righteous and faithful to be called, as the Apostle says: You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord (Eph. 5:8). But this light was made: but there was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world (John 1:9), which was not made, but born of God. That light was not made, and through the light not made this [light] was made. So also the firmament: just as light was made by the God who shines, so the firmament was made by the God who is firm. And we find that in the Church the firmament must be understood as the authority of the divine Scriptures: and therefore first light, afterwards the firmament; because Scripture was made through righteous men, and unless they were first justified, so as to be light, Scripture could not be spread abroad, so as to become a firmament between waters and waters, in the middle between the lower peoples of men and the upper peoples of the Angels. Why? Because the Angels do not desire to advance by the Scriptures, therefore they are not under the firmament, under the authority of the Scriptures; for they contemplate the very form of the godhead and of wisdom. But we are rightly under the firmament, to whom the will of God is opened through the authority of the Scriptures, etc.
The sea and the dry land. The grass of pasture.

2. We see the earth, we see the sea; they are works of God: these lie before our eyes, those lie before our understanding; these are known to our flesh, those are known to our mind. What is the dry land in the Church? Every soul thirsting for God is called dry land. For the waters were separated, and the dry land appeared. The sea is this world, and the wicked are bitter waters; they have been separated and gathered into one gathering, that is, predestined to one end, to which God directs all whom he separates from the saints. But it is God who separates; for man cannot separate these: and the dry land appears through the separation. Put two men side by side; one longs for the show, the other for the church. Joined in body, they are separated by their longings. The one belongs to the bitter water, in the other the dry land appears. How do we prove that this earth, which signifies men longing for good things, is dry? The Psalm said to God: My soul is to you like land without water (Ps. 142:6), my soul has thirsted for you. It thirsts, it is dry: it has been separated from the waters of the sea. Let no one heed that it has not yet been separated in body: already longing has made the separation. Some long for God, others long for the world. What then does the dry land thirst for? Rain from heaven, rain from the clouds, rain from the Scriptures, rain from the firmament. And when it longs for rain, it longs for sweet water, separated from the bitter water. But God knows that the dry land longs: for it is hidden and in secret. The longings of the sea, that is, worldly longings, are visible. If someone longs for money, he is moved towards the money itself, he wants to acquire it; because money is a visible thing, his longing is visible. But whoever longs for God, his longing is hidden; because God, whom he longs for, is hidden: he is within, he is a hidden thing. It thirsts indeed, and it is dry; but it is visible to the eyes of God. And he did not pass over the fruit; at once he said, Let the earth bring forth the grass of pasture. Let the earth bring forth on the very day on which it became dry land. That dry land could not be long without fruit. Let us too hear the word of God: and let the earth bring forth the grass of pasture, that is, the good works of mercy, of which Isaiah says, Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy without shelter into your house, etc. (Isa. 58:7). The firmament, then, is the Scripture of God: the lights in the firmament, the understanding of the Scriptures; and the lights in heaven, the understanding in the Scriptures. Do you want to come to the heavenly light? First be earth that gives fruit, that is, let works of mercy go before: for after works of mercy comes the illumination of that light which you long for, etc.
The greater light and the lesser light.

3. And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night. The Evangelists are the lights, the Scripture of God the firmament. And the Gospel, which has testimony from the Law and the Prophets, is the lights in the firmament of heaven. But the little one in the Church cannot yet take solid food, but is content with milk, which the lesser light and the stars signify. And therefore the greater light is for the rule of the day, the lesser light for the rule of the night. As long as men are carnal and cannot think of that wisdom through which all things were made, they are in night: but he did not abandon the night; he provided faith. For God did not abandon the night; he gave it its own lights. The day seeks the sun, the sun suffices it: the moon and stars were given to the night, they light it; and when the moon does not shine upon the earth, the light that is in the air is from the stars. Hence it comes about that we go out of doors at night and see trees; and if we do not make them out clearly, still we see somehow the light of the stars: and therefore when the clouds are thick, even the light of the stars is taken away, and a man is in the open air (a) just as he is in a bedroom. So the night too has a certain light of its own. Let us see what the Apostle says about those gifts, those spiritual endowments: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for profit. How is it given? To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge (1 Cor. 12:7-8). Whoever understands what the difference is between the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge has understood what the difference is between the greater light and the lesser light. Let us hear the word of wisdom: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning, etc. For those who grasp it, it is day, the sun shines for them: but unless [they had come] first from night, they did not come to the light; for darkness was over the abyss, and God said, Let there be light. Let no one say that he began from light. For we are all justified from being sinners. Let those who can, then, grasp what I have said about the Gospel. But they say to me, 'We have not understood what In the beginning was the Word is.' If, then, it is still night, consider that the Word took on flesh and made for you, as it were, a night-light. For the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1-3, 14). And in the bush God speaks to Moses through an angel. Hear where the word of wisdom is. 'What are you called?' said Moses; 'how shall I announce you to the people? If it is said, Who sent you? what shall I say?' Hear the word of wisdom: You shall say to the children of Israel, He who is has sent me to you. Who can grasp He who is? Other things truly are not. Who truly is? He who does not pass away, who always remains unchangeable. But this is food for the grown, this is the sun of the day. And as if Moses said to him, 'I am still night, give light to the night': 'I will say something that the night can grasp, I will say something that little ones can retain: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' So, I am who I am (Exod. 3:14-15) is for the rule of the day; I am the God of Abraham, for the rule of the night. Faith, dispensed in time, gives light to the night; wisdom, always abiding, gives light to the day. He nourishes in the night so that we may go forward into the day. The other gifts, then, are the stars. For when he had said, To one is given the word of wisdom, as the sun for the rule of the day, to another is given the word of knowledge, as the moon for the rule of the night, he gives the stars too: to another the gift of healings, to another prophecy, etc. Creeping things of living souls. The power of the sacrament is charity.

4. God said, Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls, and flying things. And the waters brought forth fishes, and great whales, and the flying things of heaven. And God saw that it is good, etc. Let us see, then, what the Scriptures say. Light through light, the righteous through the Word. The firmament of heaven, the solid support of the Scriptures. The waters under the firmament, the earthly people; the waters above the firmament, the heavenly people. The dry land separated from the waters of the sea, souls thirsting for God [separated] from the multitude of the sins of the world. The earth brings forth the grass of pasture and fruit-bearing trees, the works of mercy. The lights in the firmament of heaven, the preachers of the word, the Evangelists and Apostles, the spiritual gifts. Let us attend, then, to the lights going around the whole world, and see how the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls. The Evangelists run to and fro, men are evangelized. So the creeping things of living souls are understood as the Sacraments. Why? Because the Sacraments are necessary for this, that the Gentiles may be evangelized, and men separated from the Gentiles; that is, that those bitter waters may bring forth, and sweet fishes come to be. For it is a great thing: no one can taste the water of the sea, [yet everyone can] eat the fish: they are born in bitterness, and thrive. These are the sweet Sacraments, which have been sent through the whole world. But they are called creeping things of living souls: not yet a living soul. Why? This is somewhat dense to understand. You heard just now, when the reading was read, that Simon Magus was baptized, and did not lay aside his evil mind (Acts 8:13-23): he had the form of the Sacrament, he did not have the power of the Sacrament. Hear what the Apostle says of the ungodly: Having, he says, the form of godliness, but denying its power (2 Tim. 3:5). What is the form of godliness? The visible Sacrament. What is the power of godliness? Invisible charity. Hear the power of godliness: If I speak with the tongues of men and of Angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass, etc. And if I have this and that, but do not have charity, I am nothing (1 Cor. 13:1-3). For the Sacraments are holy and great: but a man is nothing if he does not have charity. So the power of the Sacrament is charity. This charity the heretic does not have, though I find with him the form of the Sacrament. Therefore when a heretic comes to me, I defer to the form of the Sacrament, so as not to rebaptize; but I restore the power of the Sacrament, so as to implant the root of charity. That, then, will be the living soul which the earth brings forth, so that it may be a living soul, now having the power of the Sacrament. This, then, is what was said, Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls, etc.
The creation of the living soul. The living soul. Godliness, a power. Charity. Man in the image of God.

5. God also said, Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind, etc. On the sixth day God said, Let the earth bring forth the living soul: not creeping things of living souls, but the living soul. And the earth brought forth all cattle, and beasts, and serpents, and whatever creeps upon the earth. And God saw that it is good. And God said, on the same sixth day, when the earth put forth the living soul, Let us make man in our image and likeness, etc. We have said that God made light, that is, all the faithful; he made a firmament in the world, the heaven between waters and waters; he made a firmament in the Church, the authority of the Scriptures between the peoples of the Angels, for whom this is not necessary, and the peoples of men, who were to seek God there. God made in the world the separation of the sea from the land; God made in the Church the separation of the Gentiles from his servants. The dry land thirsts for rain; men in the Church thirst for heavenly rain. The earth brought forth the grass of pasture and fruit-bearing trees; men in the Church too bring forth works of mercy. Lights come to be in heaven: the greater light, the word of wisdom; the lesser light, the word of knowledge; the stars, the gifts of healings, prophecy, faith, etc.; all these in the firmament of heaven. So when they had begun to walk and travel through the whole world, the waters generated, that is, there arose from the Gentiles creeping things of living souls, the holy Sacraments; and consecrated men having the form: for the form of the Sacrament is in a man, and sometimes the power of the Sacrament follows at once, but now in the earth which has been separated; therefore the earth brings forth the living soul. And truly, brothers, there is need to be a living soul. The brothers have received Baptism; let the power follow the form. Let Baptism not be for judgement, but for salvation. It was for judgement to Simon Magus, for salvation to Peter. Let us see, then, what the living soul is, which the earth brought forth. Consider a man: he has a body, he has a soul. In that soul he has many motions like the beasts; and he has something else, I do not know what, which the beasts do not have. What motions does he have like the beasts? Eating and drinking, sleeping and waking, and begetting. Are these not common to us with the beasts? Whoever throws these motions into self-indulgence has a dead soul, not a living soul. How do we prove it? Hear the Apostle: But she who lives in pleasures is dead while living (1 Tim. 5:6). What is living in pleasures, if not to slacken those motions of the soul which we have in common with cattle into pleasures and immoderate desires, into gluttony, into drunkenness, into fornication, into sleepiness? Those who live thus live in pleasures; but though alive they are dead. But if all these affections are restrained, and these motions are held to chastity, to continence, the earth brings forth a soul; which, since it was dead in pleasures, it remains that, reined in from pleasures, it begins to live and to have the power of godliness. And what is the power of godliness? Charity towards God and neighbour. Whoever has charity, and through faith reins in all lusts, all desires, all the motions of his mind which he has in common with cattle, will be a living soul. And it follows that now man is formed in the image and likeness of God. He is formed when all these things that have been said are brought together into that man. For both 'God made light' was said of man in the Church; and 'he made the firmament': for man's sake, the authority of the Scriptures; and 'he separated the waters from the land': the Gentiles from the believers; and 'the earth brought forth the grass of pasture': works of mercy; and 'lights in heaven': the holy Evangelists in man; and 'the earth brought forth the creeping thing of living souls': the Sacraments, and this in men; afterwards it brought forth the living soul: the reining in of all lusts, and this in man. Join all these together in understanding, and man has been made in the image and likeness of God. Note how we prove this. For this reason he said of each thing, God saw that it is good. But when he made a better thing, he did not see that it had been made better. Rather, in man himself he brings together all things that were made, and it was said, God saw all things that he had made, and behold, they were very good. All along he had said of each thing that it was good; when man had been made, he named all things. It is understood that all those single things are found in man. Do you seek light in man? You find faith. Do you seek the firmament? You find the authority of the Scriptures. Do you seek the separation of the waters? You find the faithful man separated from the Gentiles. Do you seek grass and fruit-bearing trees springing up? You find good works, works of mercy. Do you seek the lights of heaven? You find the Evangelists. Do you seek creeping things of living souls? You find the Sacraments. Do you seek the living soul? You find continence. Do you seek man in man? You find the image and likeness of God.
From the Sermon on the Fiftieth Day after the Resurrection, Florus on 1 Cor. 1.

The Lord Christ was humbled so that we might learn to be humble: he who contains all things was conceived, he who begets all things was born, he who gives life to all things died; but after three days he rose again, and ascended into heaven, and set the human flesh which he had taken up at the right hand of the Father. It is wonderful, brothers, and this is what the ungodly refuse to believe; it is wonderful that a man rose again in the flesh, and ascended into heaven with the flesh: but it is far more wonderful that the whole world believed so incredible a thing. Which is more incredible: that God did such things, or that the world was able to believe? What if we also consider the very manner in which the world believed? That too is seen to be truly divine, and is found to be exceedingly wonderful. Men untaught in the liberal disciplines, and wholly unpolished as far as the learning of the world is concerned, not skilled in grammar, not armed with dialectic, fishermen, very few of them, did Christ send with the nets of faith to the sea of the world. Why do I say very few? He sent twelve; and yet through them he so filled the Churches with every kind of fish that very many even of the wise of the world, to whom the cross of Christ seemed shameful, are signed with it on the forehead; and the thing they thought one should blush at, and for which they mocked us, they set on the citadel of shame.
From the Sermon on the Apostle Paul, at the conversion of a certain pagan Faustus, Florus on Rom. 14.

The heart of a man we can neither see nor show. God says, 'What is open is for you; what is hidden is for me.' The Apostle Paul says, 'Brothers, do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes and lights up the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the thoughts of hearts; and then each one will have praise from God' (1 Cor. 4:5). You cannot look into the heart of a new Christian. What, can you look into the heart of an old Christian? You are going to say, 'But he believed out of necessity.' That could also be said of the man of whom we were speaking a little before, 'who was formerly a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and insolent' (1 Tim. 1:13). For on him too a certain necessity was imposed: he was thrown to the ground by a voice from heaven; so that he might have light, he lost his light. Threaten whatever you like, and give as much as you like to any man: what is sweeter than this light? Yet unless Paul had lost it, he would not have received the eternal [light]. He believed out of necessity. What did he fear? Let someone tell me what he feared. Sheep crying out? Sheep can cry out; they cannot bite. Even in the very crying of God's sheep he could have noticed the glory of God, and feared the judgement of God. He was roused from a kind of sleep, so as to consider that what was foretold of Christ is fulfilled concerning Christ, that the name of Christ has such power, that the glory of God so prevails. So I say briefly to your Charity; I address the Church of God, I address the people of God: if he believed, you have found [him]; if he was afraid, you have won. Meanwhile, brothers, as far as men are able, let us not claim for ourselves beyond what has been granted. The Apostle says: 'Receive him who is weak in faith, not in judgements of thoughts' (Rom. 14:1). Let us not claim for ourselves the judging of other people's thoughts: but let us offer our thoughts to God, even on behalf of those about whom we perhaps have some doubt. Perhaps his very newness is somewhat in doubt. Love the doubter all the more: by your love cure the doubt from the heart of the weak man. Look at the inner face, in which you may rejoice; commit the heart to God, and pray for it. Know that he is being abandoned by the wicked and taken up by you. Love the man more than you formerly hated the error. So Christ came to heal the sick, as we heard from the Gospel: 'For it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill' (Matt. 9:12). 'And what man is there who, when he has lost one sheep, does not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains, and go to look for the one that was lost, and when he has found it rejoices over it? So my Father rejoices over one who repents, rather than over ninety-nine righteous who have no need of repentance' (ibid. 18:12-14, and Luke 15:4-7). Precisely so Christ came to heal the sick; so he knows how to take merciful vengeance on his enemies. Those who shared his error, whose minds perhaps are grieved, are angry for the moment; afterwards perhaps they will imitate [him]. So, brothers, we commend him to your prayers, and to your love, and to your most faithful friendship, and to your taking up of his weakness. As you go before, so he follows: teach the good way, let him find it good in you. Now that he has become a Christian, let him discern what difference there is between what he has left and what he has found. Later times will prove his life and his zeal for the faith of Christ: but now, my brothers, it was not necessary, it was not the counsel of shepherds, to drive away one who was knocking, to put off one who was seeking. To want to judge the hidden things of the heart and not to accept an open declaration was neither [our] counsel nor our purpose. For we know how that merciful avarice of God threatens, as he seeks profit from his money everywhere, and says to the lazy servant who wanted to judge what he did not see, and was sluggish about gathering profit for his Lord: 'Wicked servant, out of your own mouth I condemn you. You said I was a hard man, reaping where I did not sow, gathering where I did not scatter: so you knew my avarice. You should have given my money to the money-changers, and on coming I would have demanded it with interest' (Luke 19:22-23). So we could do nothing but pay out the Lord's money. He will be the one who exacts, not of him only, but of all of us. Let us therefore fulfil the office of the dispenser, and not usurp the place of the exactor. So, my brothers, keep in mind the work of God: you were seeking one thing, planning another, and found another. We commend the Lord's work, servants to fellow servants. Let us love in him what our Lord has done more than what we wanted to do. For his works are better. And we heard his great and devout declaration: 'I do not want high office, I want to be a Christian.' Be glad, exult, love more than you hated. Commend his work to Christ in your prayers: show a faithful, devoted, friendly spirit to an old man's first lessons. For what does it matter that you see him already advanced in age? He came to the vineyard at the ninth hour, to receive an equal wage, etc.
From the Sermon on the Feast of Saint Quadratus, Bede, not yet published, on 2 Cor. 4.

The blessed Apostle Paul brought forward a testimony from the Scriptures, in which he commended to us the glory of the martyrs. 'Because it is written,' he says, 'I believed, therefore I have spoken. And we believe, therefore we also speak' (2 Cor. 4:13). For if they had only believed, and did not speak, they would not have suffered. By believing they laid hold of life, and by speaking they found death; but a death in which the corruptible body would be sown, and incorruption reaped. This sense, that is, 'we believe, therefore we also speak', the same Apostle explained thus in another place: 'With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation' (Rom. 10:10). From the Sermon on the Three Rods, Bede and Florus on 1 Cor. 1.

But why the Lord first chose low-born men, few, unskilled and unpolished, when he had before his eyes a great crowd, fewer indeed in comparison with those poorer men, but many of their own kind, rich, noble, learned, wise, whom he afterwards also gathered in, the Apostle sets out the mystery: 'God chose the weak things of this world to confound the strong; and God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the wise; and God chose the low-born things of this world, and the things that are not', that is, are not counted, 'so that the things that are might be brought to nothing' (1 Cor. 1:27-28). For he had come to teach humility and to overthrow pride. God had come humble: in no way would he who had come so humble seek out the lofty here first. First, because he chose to be born of that woman who was betrothed to a carpenter. So he did not choose an exalted birth, lest nobility should be proud on this earth. He did not even choose to be born in a very large city, but was born in Bethlehem of Judah, which is not even called by the name of city. To this day the inhabitants of that place call it a village: so small, so slight, it is almost nothing, were it not ennobled by the former birth of the Lord Christ. So he chose the weak, the poor, the unlearned: not because he passed over the first, the rich, the wise, the noble; but if he had chosen those first, they would seem to themselves to have been chosen on the merit of their riches, on the merit of their property, on the merit of their birth, and, puffed up by these things, they would not receive the salvation of humility, without which no one can return to that life from which we would not have fallen except through pride.
Again from the Sermon on the Three Rods, Bede, not yet published, on 1 Thess. 2.

'I became a little one in your midst, like a nurse cherishing her own children' (1 Thess. 2:7). He did not say 'mother' for this reason, that sometimes mothers are either too delicate or love their children less, and when they have given birth hand them over to others to be nursed. Again, if he had said only 'like a nurse cherishing', and had not added 'her own children', he would seem to have received children borne by another woman, to nurse. And he called himself a nurse because he fed [them]; and 'her own children', because he had borne them himself, saying: 'My children, with whom I am in labour again, until Christ is formed anew in you' (Gal. 4:19). But he gives birth as the Church gives birth, in her womb, not by her own seed.
From the Sermon on the Good of Marriage, Bede and Florus on 1 Cor. 7.

'Let him who can receive it, receive it' (Matt. 19:12). 'But I cannot,' he says. You cannot? I cannot. Then let a certain nurturing authority of the Apostle take you up: that if they do not contain themselves, they should marry. Let something be done by which one may come to pardon. Let it belong to pardon, so that one does not rush into eternal punishment. Let what is lawful be done, by which what is unlawful may be forgiven. This is shown by what follows: 'I would rather they marry than burn' (1 Cor. 7:9). He conceded something, I say, to incontinence because he feared something greater: he feared eternal punishments, he feared what awaits and remains for adulterers. Even this, that married people, overcome by desire, make use of one another beyond the need of begetting children, I will place among those things for which it is said daily, 'Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors' (Matt. 6:12).

From the Sermon on what is written in Matt. 16:24, 'If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself': Bede, not yet published, on 1 Thess. 5, 'Rebuke the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted', etc.

When someone sees a person living badly, who perhaps provides something for the Church, and does not rebuke him, he flees in spirit. What is it to flee in spirit? To be afraid. Fear is an inward flight. Why is he afraid? Because he is a hireling. [He fears] lest that person take it badly that he is rebuked, and not give what he usually gives. He sees the wolf coming, that is, the devil breaking the neck of the one who lives badly; and he flees in spirit, he holds back from a useful rebuke, full of fear. But he who is a shepherd, and has care for the sheep, does not let him go, and does what the Apostle says: 'Rebuke the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted', etc. So let no one think a shepherd, or one who calls himself a shepherd, devoted because he does not return evil for evil, when he rather returns evil for good. For that man, even if he is a wicked sinner, gives to the Church from his goods; but this one returns evil for good to him from whom he withholds rebuke. But since all this must be done out of love, and sometimes people think those who rebuke them are their enemies, therefore, when he had said, 'Rebuke the unruly', he added, 'comfort the faint-hearted'. For perhaps he begins to lose heart because of the rebuke, and is troubled: then you ought to comfort him. 'Support the weak', so that they do not fall through weakness. If weakness has made him stagger, let charity take him up in her bosom. And when he had said these things, he added at the end, 'See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone' (1 Thess. 5:14–15). Therefore rebuke is not an evil, if there is [rebuke]. But the good sheep, when it is rebuked by its overseer, what does it say? 'The righteous man will correct me in mercy' (Ps. 140:5).
From the Sermon on what the Lord says, Luke 11:10, 'Ask and you will receive': Bede, not yet published, on 2 Cor. 12.

We find that the wicked have asked and received, and the good have asked and not received. For what is worse than demons? And yet they asked for the pigs and received [them] (Matt. 8:31–32). And God is found not to have done the desire of the Apostles, and to have fulfilled the desire of the demons. What then do we say, except that 'the Lord knows who are his' (2 Tim. 2:19), and every one of them who asks receives? But a scruple still remains about the Apostle; for surely he who spoke this sentence, 'The Lord knows who are his', was not himself outside the number of those who are his. Therefore all who are his ask and receive. But we ask: what? For those things that are asked for the sake of this temporal life sometimes profit, sometimes harm; and when God knows that they harm, he does not give them to his own who desire and ask for them: just as a doctor does not give whatever the sick man has asked for; and by loving he refuses what by not loving he would grant. So he hears all his own for eternal salvation; he does not hear all for temporal desire; and so he does not hear for this, in order to hear for that. Finally, consider the very words too. When he did not receive that for which he asked the Lord three times, [the Lord] said to him: 'My grace is sufficient for you; for power is made perfect in weakness' (2 Cor. 12:9). Why do you desire from me that the thorn of the flesh be taken from you, which you received so that you would not be exalted in your revelations? Surely you ask this because you do not know what profits you. Trust the doctor: what he has applied is sharp, but useful; it causes pain, but brings forth health. Power is made perfect in weakness. Endure weakness, then, if you desire health: endure weakness, if you desire perfection, because power is made perfect in weakness.
From the Sermon on the words of the Apostle, 'Our struggle is not', etc. Bede and Florus on Eph. 6.

'Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.' Because it is not only a man who persecutes you, but the devil through him; and before he harms you in the body, he kills himself in the heart. 'Our struggle is not against flesh and blood', [that is,] for men against men, who are flesh and blood: 'but against principalities and powers, the rulers of this darkness' (Eph. 6:12); because just as Christ governs and rules those who are light, so the devil drives and incites those who are darkness to every evil. This, then, the Apostle urges on us: that we pray not against the evil man, but against the devil who works with him; and that we do whatever we can so that the devil may be driven out and the man set free. For just as, if an armed man from the opposing side comes, seated on a horse, against someone stationed in battle, he is angry not with the horse but with the rider; and as far as he can, he strives to do this, to strike the rider and take possession of the horse: so one must act towards evil men; and one must labour with all one's strength not against them, but against him who incites them; so that, while the devil is conquered, that unhappy man whom he had begun to possess may be set free.
From the same Sermon, Bede and Florus on 1 Cor. 12.

'He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked' (1 John 2:6). What is this way in which Christ walked? What else is it but charity, of which the Apostle says, 'I show you a still more excellent way' (1 Cor. 12:31)? If then we wish to imitate Christ, we ought to run along that very way which Christ deigned to walk even when hanging on the cross. For he was nailed to the cross, and running the way of charity, he made supplication for his persecutors. Indeed, this is what he said: 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34). So let us too constantly make this supplication for all our enemies, that the Lord may grant them amendment of their ways and pardon of their sins.
From the Sermon, 'What a bishop ought to be', and where Paul rebukes Peter: Bede, not yet published, on 1 Tim. 3.

'A bishop, then, must be beyond reproach' (1 Tim. 3:2). Who denies this? But though a bishop must be beyond reproach, is it fitting for a Christian to be open to reproach? 'Bishop' is a Greek word: in Latin it can be called 'overseer' or 'visitor'. We are bishops, but with you we are Christians. We are named specifically from visiting: all are named in common from anointing. If the anointing is common, the contest too is common. But why do we visit, if there is nothing good that we may see in you?
From the Sermon on the Sabbath, Florus on 2 Cor. 3.

'But when he has turned to God, the veil will be taken away.' The veil is done away with, not Moses: the veil, not the law. Consider how the Lord came, and the veil is done away with: when he hung on the tree, the veil was torn. O great mystery! O ineffable sacrament! The transgressors of the law crucified [him], and the secrets of the law were laid open. Was not that cross the key of the Lord? He held [it], and opened what was shut. But the Jews, even with the veil torn, have their face covered. 'But we,' says the Apostle, 'with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord' (2 Cor. 3:16, 18).
From the Sermon on the Kalends of January against the Pagans, John the Deacon on Leviticus.

The Apostle Peter says to the Church, which is the body of Christ: 'A holy people, a royal priesthood' (1 Pet. 2:9). For then one priest was anointed; now all Christians are anointed. The king was anointed, and the priest was anointed; the rest were not anointed. The Lord bore both roles, not in figure but now in truth, both of king and of priest. For this reason the Apostle says of the Lord himself, 'Who was made for him of the seed of David according to the flesh' (Rom. 1:3). See, then, the royal lineage. So Christ is said to be of the seed of David because of Mary, since she was of the seed of David. But what lineage [was] in Mary? It is written in the Gospel that the priest Zechariah had a wife Elizabeth of the daughters of Aaron. So [she was] of priestly lineage, since that whole tribe of Levi [was so]. And in the Gospel the angel says to the Virgin Mary, 'Your kinswoman Elizabeth' (Luke 1:36). If then Elizabeth, one of the daughters of Aaron the priest, was Mary's kinswoman, there is no doubt that the Virgin Mary belonged not only to royal but also to priestly blood. Therefore both roles, royal and priestly, are present in the Lord according to the man whom he assumed. This is why at that time two were anointed in figure, king and priest: because it was fulfilled in him, our head, whose body, it is clear, we the whole Church are. Hence we are rightly called a royal and priestly race.
Likewise from the Sermon on the Kalends of January against the Pagans, John the Deacon, in the same place.

In those ancient sacraments our one Lord Jesus Christ was prefigured. One priest used to enter the holy of holies, but all the people stood outside. Now, when the bishops stand at the altar, are you outside, and not inside? At that time one priest entered the holy of holies once a year. The year signifies the whole of time. So once in the whole of time our one priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead, entered the holy of holies, not figurative but true, beyond the veils of the heavens, offering himself for us. He entered, and he is there. But the people still stand outside with us: we have not yet risen to go out to meet Christ and to remain always within with him, when he will say to the good servant, 'Enter into the joy of your Lord' (Matt. 25:21). This, then, was figured at that time by one priest entering alone into the holy of holies and the people standing outside, which has now been fulfilled through our Lord Jesus Christ entering alone above the secret places of the heavens, and the people still groaning outside, saved in hope, awaiting the redemption of their body, which will come in the resurrection of the dead.
Likewise from the Sermon on the Kalends of January against the Pagans, John the Deacon, in the same place.

For he himself, the high priest, offers our prayers, he who offered himself as a burnt offering for us. He it is who leads us through, placing himself between, not to shut [us] off but to direct [us]; not to separate but to reconcile; not to hinder but to break apart the hindrances. He is the one high priest and the one priest who was prefigured in the ancient priests of God. That is why a priest without blemish of body was sought: because he alone lived without blemish of sin, even in mortal flesh. For what was prefigured in their body was signified as to come in his life.
